weaknesses: Conceptual framing issues: Labeling as 'criminal potential' anthropomorphizes and sensationalizes; these are harmful generation patterns in role-play, not intrinsic properties. 'Vulnerability to generating harmful behaviors' would be more precise

Methodological problem: GPT-4o serves as both evaluated model and gold-standard judge in God perspective, creating circularity. While 20% human validation mitigates this, the dependency on a single model's judgments for other models' evaluation is problematic

Intent inference: Trait definitions require detecting 'intent' with formal requirements for explicit mention in thought segments. This biases toward easily-articulated intentions, may miss implicit harm, and introduces subjective judgment despite 'strict' formalization. No separate inter-annotator agreement for intent assessment reported

Limited novelty: Deception in adversarial role-play scenarios confirms prior findings (Ward et al. 2023, Park et al. 2024). Core findings about harmful outputs under explicit instruction are somewhat expected rather than surprising

Statistical concerns: Correlation r=-0.776 with n=8 models is underpowered; no significance testing or confidence intervals reported across comparisons; uneven sample sizes across models

No mitigation strategies evaluated: Paper identifies vulnerabilities but doesn't test potential solutions (adversarial training, decoding constraints, safety modules). Limited actionable guidance for practitioners
Overly strict OTDA metric: Exact-match trait sets penalize near-misses (4/5 correct = 0 score). Per-trait F1 scores (in appendix) would be more informative and nuanced
Limited scope: 60 scenarios is modest; 8 LLMs only (all text-based); crime domain narrow; English-only; may not generalize to other harmful contexts (misinformation, harassment, bias)
